477.title: Omniscience — and the invitation of the gods, refused (3.49–3.51)
477.hook: discernment brings knowing everything, and the next step is letting even that go; then the gods arrive with an invitation, and the yogi says no
477.howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras often tell the Bhashya's scene of the gods' invitation to warn students against both attachment and pride in their progress, and Hindu stories praise renunciants who turn down heavenly rewards for the sake of liberation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: indriya-jaya, and your line, the senses. From the known to the knowing. Did you notice the tasting more than the taste? Today, the knower. Day four hundred seventy-seven.

The classical commentary tells it as a scene. A yogi sits in practice, far along now, close to the end. And the gods arrive. Not demons, not tempters in disguise. Gods, the beings of the high places, warm and respectful. Sir, sit here. Enjoy yourself here. This pleasure is lovely. This elixir holds back age and death. Here's a chariot that flies. Here are trees that grant every wish. Come and stay. Generous, polite, and sincere. Today's sutras say what the yogi does next.
screen: `THE GODS ARRIVE.` → `SIT HERE. ENJOY HERE.` → `COME AND STAY.`

segments.voice: First the summit. Sutra 3.49: for the one who sees only the difference between the mind's clearest part and the seer, mastery over all states of being, and knowing everything. Omniscience. Sarva-jnatritva. This is discernment, which we met three weeks ago, carried all the way. Then sutra 3.50, a bold line. By dispassion even toward that, the seeds of every fault are destroyed, and freedom comes. Kaivalya. Even toward that. Even omniscience gets set down. Then 3.51. When invited by those in the high places, don't be attached, and don't be proud, because unwanted things could return. Two dangers, not one. Attachment: you might say yes. And pride: you might say no, and then think, the gods themselves came to invite me. The commentary gives the yogi's answer as a reflection. I've been roasted on the coals of rebirth, tossed in the dark, and now I've found the lamp of yoga. Why would I let these sweet things be the wind that blows it out? So the yogi refuses. Quietly. No speech, no triumph. Notice who's at the door. Not enemies. Gods, and good things: long life, beauty, ease. A generous invitation can be harder to turn down than a hostile one. And on an ordinary Tuesday? The invitation is rarely a flying chariot. It's the comfortable stopping place, just short of what you set out to do.
screen: `SARVA-JNATRITVA: KNOWING EVERYTHING.` · `DISPASSION, EVEN TOWARD THAT.` · `NO ATTACHMENT. NO PRIDE.` · `THE LAMP AND THE WIND.` · then, large: `REFUSE THE INVITATION.`

segments.voice: Today's practice notices the comfortable stopping places. Sit steady and easy, and rest on the breath. After a while, something pleasant will invite you away: a daydream, a plan for later, a drowsy warmth. Notice it like a kind visitor at the door. You don't have to be rude to it. Just thank it, silently, and stay with the breath. If a little pride follows at having stayed, greet it the same way, and let it pass. The bell holds the time.
Omniscience. Knowing everything, which comes from full discernment, and which Patanjali says to let go of too.
Your line: refuse the invitation. Today, when a comfortable reason to stop short shows up, decline it kindly once, without feeling proud that you did. Day four hundred seventy-seven.

478.title: Discernment of the moment (3.52–3.54)
478.hook: samyama on the single instant and the order of instants brings the knowledge that carries you across
478.tomorrow: Kaivalya — when purity of mind equals purity of self
478.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras study 3.52–3.54 with the classical commentary's account of the instant, and in meditation practitioners often train attention on the present moment of the breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday: omniscience, and your line, refuse the invitation. The gods at the door, declined without clinging and without pride. Did you turn down one comfortable stopping place? Day four hundred seventy-eight.

Two gooseberries sit on a table. Same size, same green, same tiny freckle near the stem. You look at them, then step out of the room. While you're gone, someone swaps them. You come back. Which is which? Nothing on the surface says. The classical commentary uses exactly this puzzle, two identical fruits, to explain today's sutras. And its answer is that someone with the right kind of discernment could tell them apart. Not by color or shape. By time.
screen: `TWO IDENTICAL GOOSEBERRIES.` → `SWAPPED WHILE YOU WERE OUT.` → `WHICH IS WHICH?`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.52: by samyama on the moment and its sequence, knowledge born of discernment. The word for moment is kshana, the instant. The commentary makes it vivid. As the atom is the smallest piece of matter, the instant is the smallest piece of time. And sequence, krama, is just instants following one another without a break. Then the commentary says something startling. An hour, a day, a year: those are put together by the mind. They don't exist out there as things. Only one instant is real at a time. The whole world changes in that single instant, and the past and future are carried in it as what has been and what will be. Then sutra 3.53: from this, you can tell apart two things that look the same, that share kind, marks and place. The two gooseberries. Each one has its own line of instants, its own history, moment after moment. Rest samyama on that, and the swap is plain. Sutra 3.54 names this knowledge. Taraka, the one that carries across, like a ferry over a river. It takes everything as its object, in every way, and it's without sequence. All at once. Not one thing after another, the way the mind usually knows. So book three's tour of powers ends here, not with flying or vanishing, but with seeing the single instant clearly. And there's an ordinary version. Much of what weighs on a person is an hour, a week, a year, piled up in the mind. The instant itself is often light.
screen: `KSHANA: THE SMALLEST PIECE OF TIME.` · `AN HOUR IS PUT TOGETHER BY THE MIND.` · `EACH FRUIT HAS ITS OWN LINE OF INSTANTS.` · `TARAKA: THE ONE THAT CARRIES ACROSS.` · then, large: `THE INSTANT.`

segments.voice: Today's practice rests in the instant. Sit steady and easy. Notice the breath, not this breath as a whole, but this instant of it, the tiny touch of air right now. Then this one. Then this one. When the mind builds something bigger, the rest of the day, the week, notice the building, and come back to this single instant. Light as it is. The bell holds the time.
Taraka, the knowledge that carries across, like a ferry over a river. By samyama on the instant and its sequence, this is what discernment of the moment becomes.
Your line: the instant. Today, when a day feels too heavy, shrink it, not to the hour, not to the minute, but to this one instant, and see what's actually in it. Day four hundred seventy-eight.

479.title: Kaivalya — when purity of mind equals purity of self (3.55–3.56)
479.hook: the book of powers ends not with a power but with a cleaned window: when the mind is as pure as the seer, there is freedom
479.tomorrow: The powers by birth, herbs, mantra, discipline, samadhi
479.howItsDone: In the Yoga tradition, kaivalya is the goal of practice: the seer standing free of entanglement with nature, reached through discernment and dispassion, and teachers stress that it does not depend on gaining any powers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: taraka, and your line, the instant. Only one instant is real at a time. Did a heavy day get lighter when you shrank it to now? Day four hundred seventy-nine.

Somewhere there's a sliding glass door so clean that people walk straight into it. You've seen it, maybe done it. The glass is still there. It still has a job, holding the weather out. But it's so clear that it no longer adds anything of its own to the garden on the other side. No smudge, no tint, no reflection of the room. You look through it and see only what's there. Book three has spent fifteen days on powers. Here is its last sutra, and it isn't a power at all. It's that door.
screen: `A GLASS DOOR SO CLEAN.` → `PEOPLE WALK INTO IT.` → `IT ADDS NOTHING OF ITS OWN.`

segments.voice: The last sutra of book three: when the purity of the mind's clearest part equals the purity of the seer, kaivalya. The mind's clearest part is sattva, the quality of light and clarity. The seer is purusha, pure awareness, which never needed cleaning. So the work has all been on one side. The glass, not the garden. Practice, discernment, letting go, all of it wipes the glass until it adds nothing of its own. And then the two are equal. Kaivalya comes from kevala, alone, only, whole. Not loneliness. More like standing on its own, needing nothing. The seer, no longer tangled with what it sees. Then the classical commentary adds a line that's easy to miss and hard to forget. This freedom comes whether or not someone has the powers. Fifteen days of invisibility, elephants, gods at the door, and the commentary quietly says: none of that was required. A plain person with a clear mind arrives at the same place. Now look back over book three. Concentration, meditation, absorption. Prajna, samyama. The transformations of the mind. Then the powers, one after another: past and future, other minds, strength, the stars, the heart. The warning in the middle. The elements, the senses, omniscience let go, the gods refused, the instant seen clearly. And at the end, not a greater power, but a cleaner window. Two purities, equal. Tomorrow, the fourth and last book, on freedom itself.
screen: `SATTVA: THE MIND'S CLEAREST PART.` · `ALL THE WORK IS ON THE GLASS.` · `KEVALA: ALONE, WHOLE.` · `WITH OR WITHOUT THE POWERS.` · `BOOK THREE, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `EQUAL.`

segments.voice: Today's practice wipes the glass a little. Sit steady and easy, and rest on the breath. Notice whatever the mind is adding right now: a mood, a commentary, a judgment about how this is going. Don't fight it. Just see it as a smudge on the glass, and let it fade on its own. Then look through again at the breath, plain and clear, as it is. Again and again, smudge, seen, clear. The bell holds the time.
Kaivalya. Aloneness, wholeness, freedom: when the mind's clarity is equal to the seer's purity.
Your line: equal. Today, catch one moment where your mood is tinting everything, and wipe the glass: see the person or the task without the tint, just once. Day four hundred seventy-nine.

480.title: The powers by birth, herbs, mantra, discipline, samadhi (4.1)
480.hook: the last book opens by listing five places powers can come from, and only one of them is samadhi
480.howItsDone: Hindu traditions recognize many sources of extraordinary ability, including birth, medicinal preparations, mantra and austerity, and teachers of the Yoga Sutras use 4.1 to remind students that such abilities are not in themselves signs of liberation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kaivalya, and your line, equal. When the mind is as clear as the seer, freedom, with or without the powers. Did you wipe the glass once? Day four hundred eighty.

A hummingbird hangs in the air outside a kitchen window, perfectly still, wings a blur. No human being has ever done that on their own. Yet the hummingbird never meditated a day in its life. It didn't fast, didn't chant, didn't study. It was born that way. Hovering is just what its body does. Hold onto that bird. Book four of the Yoga Sutras, the last and shortest book, is called Kaivalya, freedom. And its very first sutra is about where powers come from. The hummingbird is the first answer.
screen: `A HUMMINGBIRD HOVERS.` → `IT NEVER MEDITATED.` → `BORN THAT WAY.`

segments.voice: Sutra 4.1: the powers are born of birth, herbs, mantra, discipline or samadhi. Five sources. Birth: some abilities come with the body you're born into. The classical commentary speaks of powers that come with birth into another kind of body. A bird is born to fly. Herbs: the commentary mentions elixirs, potions said to be found in the realms of the asuras. Mantra: sacred sound, recited with power. Discipline, tapas: the heat of austerity. And samadhi: everything book three has been describing. Now ask why the book of freedom opens here. One answer: it puts the powers in their place. If an ability can come from birth, or from an herb, then an ability on its own proves nothing about someone's inner life. A hummingbird hovers, and nobody calls it enlightened. Patanjali has already told us the powers are obstacles in samadhi. Here he adds: they're not even unique to yoga. Five doors lead to them. Only one of those doors is samadhi. And over the next few sutras, he'll say that the mind born of meditation is the one that leaves no new karma behind. So the list isn't a menu. It's a quiet sorting. Book four is short, thirty-four sutras, and it's headed somewhere bigger than any power: the nature of mind, karma, time, and finally freedom itself. But first it clears the table. Five sources, and none of them is the point.
screen: `BIRTH, HERBS, MANTRA.` · `DISCIPLINE, AND SAMADHI.` · `A POWER ALONE PROVES NOTHING.` · `ONLY ONE DOOR IS SAMADHI.` · then, large: `FIVE SOURCES.`

segments.voice: Today's practice notices what you were simply given. Sit steady and easy, and rest on the breath. The breath itself is a gift of birth. You didn't earn it. Feel it come, without your effort. Then think of one ability you have that you never really worked for: a good ear, a quick laugh, patience with children. Hold it lightly, without pride, without dismissing it. Just: this came with me. Then come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Kaivalya, freedom, the name of the Yoga Sutras' fourth book. Its first sutra names five sources of power: birth, herbs, mantra, discipline and samadhi.
Your line: five sources. Today, when someone impresses you, or you impress yourself, ask where that ability came from before deciding what it says about anyone. Day four hundred eighty.

481.title: The mind's transformations from nature (4.2–4.6)
481.hook: real change comes from nature overflowing, and practice doesn't push the water, it only breaks the dam, like a farmer opening a channel
481.tomorrow: Karma of the yogi — neither white nor black
481.howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras often use the farmer of 4.3 to describe practice as removing obstacles rather than producing results, and some Hindus describe their discipline and worship in the same way, as clearing the way for grace or for what is already within.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kaivalya, book four, and your line, five sources. Birth, herbs, mantra, discipline, samadhi, and a power alone proves nothing. Did you ask where an ability came from? Day four hundred eighty-one.

Early morning on a farm in the plains. The canal is full. Water sits behind a low wall of packed earth at the head of a dry field. The farmer doesn't carry the water over in buckets. That would take all day, and he'd never finish. He takes one spade, cuts through the little earthen wall, and steps back. The water does the rest, running down every furrow on its own, because water runs downhill. That's all he did. One cut. Patanjali chose this farmer, of all the pictures in the world, to explain how a person changes.
screen: `A FULL CANAL.` → `ONE CUT IN THE EARTH WALL.` → `THE WATER DOES THE REST.`

segments.voice: Sutra 4.2: the transformation into another kind of being comes from the overflowing of nature. Prakriti, nature, is already full of potential, like the canal. Change is that fullness flowing into a new shape. Then sutra 4.3, the farmer. The instrumental cause doesn't set nature moving. It only pierces the barrier, like a farmer. The instrumental cause means everything you do: good deeds, practice, discipline. Patanjali's claim is that none of it pushes nature anywhere. It can't. Nature does its own flowing. What practice can do is cut the wall. The classical commentary spells it out. The farmer who wants to flood one field from another doesn't drag the water by hand. He breaks the dike, and the water flows in by itself. So in a person, practice removes what's in the way, and nature's own fullness runs in by itself. Then the sutras turn to a strange idea. Sutra 4.4: a yogi can form minds, made from I-ness alone. Sutra 4.5: one mind directs the many in their different tasks. And 4.6: of all these minds, the one born of meditation leaves no residue, no new seeds for the storehouse. We'll pick up that thread tomorrow. For today, stay with the farmer. It's a gentle picture of effort. You aren't making the water. You couldn't if you tried. You're finding the wall, and cutting it, and stepping back.
screen: `NATURE OVERFLOWING.` · `PRACTICE DOESN'T PUSH THE WATER.` · `IT PIERCES THE BARRIER.` · `THE MIND BORN OF MEDITATION.` · then, large: `THE FARMER REMOVES THE BARRIER.`

segments.voice: Today's practice looks for one small wall. Sit steady and easy, and rest on the breath. Notice whether you're pushing anything: the breath, the stillness, the feeling of doing this right. Then stop pushing. Look for what's in the way instead: tight shoulders, a clenched jaw, a worry held in the chest. Choose one, and gently let it open. Then step back, like the farmer, and let the breath run through on its own. The bell holds the time.
Kshetrika, the farmer. Change flows from nature's own fullness; practice, like a farmer, only removes the barrier.
Your line: the farmer removes the barrier. Today, instead of forcing one thing to happen, find the one wall that's in its way, cut it, and step back. Day four hundred eighty-one.

482.title: Karma of the yogi — neither white nor black (4.7)
482.hook: most people's actions come in three colors; Patanjali says the yogi's come in none
482.howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras often read 4.7 alongside the Bhagavad Gita's teaching on action without attachment to its fruit, and some practitioners try to do service quietly, without seeking credit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sutras 4.2 to 4.6: kshetrika. Your line was the farmer removes the barrier. Practice doesn't push the water; it opens the channel. Did you clear one small blockage and let something flow? Day four hundred eighty-two.

Laundry day. Three piles on the bedroom floor: the whites, the darks, and the big mixed heap that's a bit of both. Everything goes somewhere. Patanjali sorts human action the same way, by color, and he names the piles. Then, in one short line of the fourth chapter, he says something that sounds strange at first: the action of a person who has gone all the way in yoga goes in no pile at all.
screen: `THREE PILES ON THE FLOOR.` → `ACTION, SORTED BY COLOR.` → `AND ONE KIND IN NO PILE.`

segments.voice: Here's the thread, sutra 4.7: karma ashukla-akrishnam yoginas, trividham itaresham. The action of the yogi is not white and not black. For everyone else, it is of three kinds. Shukla means white, or bright. Krishna here means black, or dark. The old commentary attributed to Vyasa spells out the three. Black is action that harms. Black-and-white, mixed, is ordinary action: it does good, but it leans on outward means and touches others, so it's never perfectly clean. White is action done inwardly, through discipline, study and meditation. All three leave seeds. Bright seeds and dark seeds, but seeds, and seeds sprout. That's the surprise. For Patanjali, white karma isn't the finish line. A gold chain still holds you. So what is the fourth kind, neither white nor black? The commentators describe someone whose afflictions have worn thin, who acts without craving the fruit. The act still happens. Food gets cooked, the sick get visited. But nothing new is being sown, because nobody is standing there waiting for the harvest. If that sounds familiar, it's close to what Krishna tells Arjuna in the Gita: your right is to the work, never to its fruits. Patanjali puts it in his own terms. Action without the hook of wanting leaves no seed behind. So the line isn't saying the yogi stops caring about good and harm. It says the yogi's good is done without a hand held out.
screen: `WHITE, BLACK, AND MIXED.` · `ALL THREE LEAVE SEEDS.` · `A GOLD CHAIN STILL HOLDS YOU.` · `NEITHER: ACTION WITHOUT THE HAND OUT.` · then, large: `KARMĀŚUKLĀKṚṢṆAṂ YOGINAS TRIVIDHAM ITAREṢĀM.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one kind thing you did recently. Notice whether anything is attached to it: a wish to be thanked, to be seen as good, to have it count. Don't fight that wish. Just see it, the way you'd see a sticker left on a piece of fruit. Then let the act stand by itself, without the sticker. It happened. It was good. That's enough. Rest there with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Ashukla-akrishna, neither white nor black. The yogi's karma, done fully and left free of its fruit, so it plants no seed.
Your line: neither. Today, do one good thing that nobody will ever know about, and don't mention it, not even to yourself at the end of the day. Day four hundred eighty-two.

original.note: Sanskrit: a (not) + shukla (white) + a (not) + krishna (black). neither white nor black.

483.title: Desires are beginningless (4.10–4.11)
483.hook: you can't find the first craving, and Patanjali says you don't need to
483.tomorrow: The object exists independent of the mind (4.14–4.17)
483.howItsDone: In the yoga tradition, vasanas are worked with less by searching for their origin than by withdrawing what sustains them: practice, non-attachment and discernment, as the earlier chapters of the Yoga Sutras teach.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sutra 4.7: ashukla-akrishna. Your line was neither. Did one good thing go by today with no receipt attached? Today also closes a week. Day four hundred eighty-three.

It's eleven at night and you're standing at the open fridge, not hungry, looking for something. Or scrolling, thumb moving on its own. And a familiar question shows up: why am I like this? When did this start? Was it childhood, a hard year, something someone said? We dig for the first cause as if finding it would switch the whole thing off. Patanjali has a short, almost blunt answer to that search. There is no first one.
screen: `ELEVEN AT NIGHT, AT THE OPEN FRIDGE.` → `WHEN DID THIS START?` → `THERE IS NO FIRST ONE.`

segments.voice: Sutra 4.10: tasam anaditvam chashisho nityatvat. And they have no beginning, because the will to live is everlasting. They are the vasanas, the deep traces of desire laid down by past action. The commentary points to something we can all see: every creature, from the first breath, wants to go on. Let me not stop being. That wish has no starting date, so the traces it lays down have none either. That has a practical side. If there's no first craving, there's no one moment to blame, and no point spending years in the archive. Then sutra 4.11 turns the key. These traces are held together by four things: a cause, a result, a place to rest in the mind, and an object to lean on. Take those away and the traces go too. A campfire can burn for as long as anyone remembers. Nobody knows who lit it. It still goes out when the wood stops coming. So the practice isn't archaeology. It's noticing what is feeding the craving right now. Now the week, from the top. Omniscience offered, and the invitation of the gods refused. Discernment down to the instant. Kaivalya, when the mind's purity equals the self's. The five sources of powers. The farmer opening the channel. Action that is neither white nor black. And today: desires without a beginning, which can still have an end.
screen: `THE WILL TO LIVE HAS NO START DATE.` · `NO FIRST CRAVING TO BLAME.` · `HELD BY FOUR SUPPORTS.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `TĀSĀM ANĀDITVAṂ CĀŚIṢO NITYATVĀT.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Let a small want come up on its own: to check the phone, to shift, to get up. Don't ask where it came from. Ask what it's leaning on at this moment. A thought? A sound? An itch? Just name the support, quietly, and watch what the want does when it's seen. Then come back to the breath. If another want arrives, do the same. The bell holds the time.
Vasana, the trace desire leaves behind. These traces have no first moment, because the will to live has none, but they rest on supports, and without them they fall away.
Your line: no beginning. Today, when an old craving shows up, skip the question why am I like this, and ask what is feeding it right now. Day four hundred eighty-three.

screen: `DAY 483 COUNTS.` → `ANOTHER WEEK OF PATANJALI, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: THE OBJECT EXISTS INDEPENDENT OF THE MIND.`

original.note: Sanskrit vāsanā: a lingering trace or scent, the deep impression desire leaves behind.
